title: Routing stitch & tokenization overlap — long-context exploration
content:
Purpose:
Quick write-up of an experiment thread exploring an underinvestigated source of latency/throughput overhead in long-context MoE and dense models: the interaction between tokenization (and tokenizer batching) and routing/stitching phases in the runtime. Goal is to capture observations, microbenchmarks, and concrete mitigations to try in the next sprint.

Top-level hypothesis:
- When we serve long-context requests (>= 8k tokens), tokenization and request pre-processing overlap awkwardly with routing and KV stitching work. For MoE, this overlap causes pipeline stalls and headroom loss because:
  1) tokenizer output (variable-length token sequences) forces dynamic batching changes late in the pipeline, invalidating precomputed routing budgets;
  2) tokenizer / byte-pair merges step on the CPU can delay enqueue time and cause small fragmented batches that are expensive for expert routing;
  3) stitching (expert KV merge + cross-device memcpy) benefits from deterministic batch shapes but suffers when token lengths vary mid-batch.

Environments tested:
- Model variants: Llama-2-70B, Mistral-22B, Qwen-34B, MoE prototype (base 16-experts, gating top-2).
- Hardware: p4d-like (A100 8x), A10G nodes, and a 4xH100 test cluster.
- Runtime branch: local profiling build with extra tracing (branch: stitch-tokenize-explore).
- Workload: two synthetic distributions: (A) uniform long context: 50% requests 12k tokens, 50% 8k tokens; (B) heavy tail: 10% 32k, 40% 16k, 50% 4k. Requests include both generation and scoring paths.

Key microbenchmarks (numbers are median over 1000 requests, p95 reported where relevant):
- Tokenizer CPU time per request (single-threaded tokenization): Llama prompts ~18–28 ms for 8k tokens; Mistral ~16–24 ms; Qwen ~20–30 ms. Heavy-tail 32k tokens tokenization hits ~85–110 ms.
- Tokenizer batching: grouping tokenization into 8-request batches (coordinator-level) amortizes CPU time to ~7–12 ms per request for 8k steady state, but increases latency tail for small requests when coordinator waits 5–12 ms to form batch.
- Enqueue-to-first-dispatch (coordinator->worker queue latency): baseline 4–6 ms; when tokenizer batching enabled + dynamic resizing triggered, it increases to 12–20 ms and variance spikes.
- Expert routing overhead (MoE): pure routing compute (gating softmax + topK) negligible relative to attention, but end-to-end routing cost including stitching and KV merging is dominated by memcpy + synchronization: p50 extra 6–10 ms, p95 up to 28 ms for long contexts.
- Stitching cost sensitivity: when batch token-length variance < 8 tokens, stitching cost stable; when variance > 64 tokens within batch, stitching memcpy overhead and alignment padding cause +12–18% latency and 9–14% extra GPU memory due to temporary buffers.

Profiling traces observations:
- Timeline shows tokenizer CPU work often ending slightly after the coordinator had scheduled I/O and pre-allocated KV buffers leading to a double allocation pattern; that wastes 7–14 ms on worker side re-alloc + cross-device page mapping on p4d.
- For MoE, gating decisions arrive early but the final expert assignment requires the full sequence length to compute token positions for KV indices; when tokenization returns late, workers stall waiting for full KV indices, which prevents overlapping attention compute with earlier data movement.
- On H100 cluster we saw lower memcpy cost (~20% less) but tokenizer CPU dominated same as on A100; i.e., faster interconnect helps but not the tokenizer stall.

Root causes (ranked):
1) Tokenizer latency is non-negligible for long contexts and is not fully overlapped with downstream pipeline.
2) Coordinator-level tokenization batching reduces CPU overall cost but increases enqueue latency variability and causes late batch-shape changes.
3) The runtime's current KV allocation strategy assumes final sequence lengths at dispatch time; it performs expensive re-allocations when shapes change.
4) MoE stitching code expects reasonably homogeneous per-request sequence lengths; heterogeneity leads to padding and temporary buffers which blow memory and latency.

Short-term mitigations to try (low effort):
- E1: Eager approximate token-length estimation using byte-length heuristics at ingress (fast) to provision KV shapes early; only adjust if tokenized_len - estimate > threshold. This reduces re-alloc rate.
- E2: Soft tokenizer batching: coordinator issues tokenization tasks but uses a small deadline (e.g., 6 ms). If batch not filled by deadline, proceed with partial batch to avoid long waits. Tunable per SLO.
- E3: Pre-allocate KV buffers to worst-case per-route but reuse within same routing group to avoid per-request reallocations for short bursts (trade memory for reduced p95).

Medium-term changes (requires code changes / experiments):
- M1: Change KV allocation path to be layered: a reusable slab allocator keyed by (model, device, route-profile) so we can cheaply satisfy different sequence-length shapes without GPU-side realloc.
- M2: Introduce early gating pass that operates on token-length-reduced representation (chunked gating) to pick candidate experts before final tokenization completes; follow up with precise gating for final indices. This can allow overlapping expert selection with tokenization.
- M3: For MoE, implement per-expert streaming merges that avoid global all-to-all memcpy by using ring-based transfers; reduce temporary buffer usage.

Experiments to run (specific):
- X1: Measure p95 latency and memory when enabling E1 + E2 vs baseline across workload A and B for each model. Metric: p95 latency, 99th, and per-GPU resident memory.
- X2: Implement a slab allocator prototype (M1 small) and test on Qwen-34B with heavy-tail workload to validate realloc reduction and memory fragmentation.
- X3: In MoE prototype, force zero-padding to uniform length within small groups (group size 4) and compare stitching cost vs current all-in-one batching; measure throughput drop from padding vs latency gain.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Tokenizer parallelization: is it safe to push tokenization to workers so that coordinator doesn't need to batch? That increases network I/O for raw text but may permit earlier enqueue. Need security review for sending raw text to many workers.
- How often do real customer workloads have the heavy-tail distribution? Our synthetic tail might be worse than production; need to instrument real-hosted API samples (privacy-preserving aggregate) to validate.
- Can we get tokenizer optimized C++ hot paths (we have a pending PR but unknown improvement for 32k tokens)?

Notes-to-self / implementation pointers:
- In tracer logs, add a short tag for "estimate_len" vs "tokenized_len" and the coordinator deadline used for soft batching.
- Hook the allocator metrics (alloc calls, realloc counts) into the existing tracing so we can correlate realloc spikes with p95.
- For MoE routing tests, include a flag to skip temporary buffer defragmentation so we can measure raw memcpy cost.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: prototype E1 (heuristic length estimator) + tracing tags; instrument on staging by 2026-02-25.
- Ethan: implement soft-tokenizer batching wrapper (E2) and a config knob per route; test with 6ms deadline. Target 2026-03-04.
- Miguel: prototype slab allocator sketch and run initial mem fragmentation traces with Qwen workload. Target 2026-03-11.
- Jaya: collect anonymized request-length distribution from hosted API for last 90 days; produce a short note on prevalence of heavy-tail. Target 2026-02-28 (needs compliance signoff).

Immediate conclusion / recommendation:
- The tokenizer <-> routing/stitching interaction is a real contributor to p95 spikes for long-context workloads, especially with MoE. Low-effort mitigations (E1/E2/E3) are promising and should be prototyped quickly; medium changes like slab allocators and streaming merges will likely be necessary if production traffic exhibits similar distributions.

Appendix: quick traces (sanitized)
- Trace A (Qwen-34B, heavy-tail): coordinator.deadline=6ms; tokenized_len=16000; estimate_len=15200; reallocs_in_worker=2; p95=312ms (baseline 338ms).
- Trace B (MoE 16-expert): tokenizer_batch=4; routing_groups=8; stitching_tmp=1.2GB; p95=428ms; when forcing group-homogeneity p95=360ms but throughput down 8%.

References / related docs:
- Related: kernel-fusion-scheduler-long-context-probe.json (looked for reusable scheduling heuristics)
- Related RFC: RFC-2025-11-long-context-routing (confluence)
- GitHub: runtime/pull/2483 (tracing additions)

Unresolved: prioritization against other Optimize initiatives (quantization runbook, caching improvements). Will sync with product on next triage.
